goal: Trace how a scalar loss becomes weight-wise gradients through the chain rule, then use the learning rate to update a model.

lessons.objective: By the end you can describe training as taking small parameter steps toward lower loss on a landscape.

beats.text: A model can be wrong in a thousand ways; picture each possible setting as a place with a different height.
If height means error, which direction should the model move when it wants to improve?
Place a point on a bowl-shaped loss curve and compare a step uphill with a step downhill.
Lower loss is downhill, but the model needs a local signal to choose a useful direction and step size.
With many parameters the bowl becomes a high-dimensional landscape, yet the walking idea still guides the algorithm.
Learning is a sequence of informed downhill moves through parameter space.

visuals.title: The explorer enters the loss valley
visuals.goal: Make high loss, low loss, and a downhill direction visible before introducing formulas.

visuals.title: One gradient step on a loss curve
visuals.goal: Let the learner inspect the loss curve and compare one gradient step from a chosen starting point.

lessons.objective: By the end you can explain what a loss function measures and why training optimizes the chosen scalar objective.

beats.text: Before choosing a direction, the model needs a scoreboard that says how wrong its prediction is.
What single quantity should improve when predictions become closer to their targets?
Compare a prediction with its target, turn their discrepancy into a scalar, and repeat across examples.
Loss is a designed objective: lower values mean better agreement according to that chosen measure.
The gradient only has meaning relative to this objective, so changing the loss changes the landscape.
Loss supplies the height of the landscape and gives the gradient something to reduce.

visuals.title: The loss scoreboard
visuals.goal: Show predictions becoming targets and the scalar loss falling.

visuals.title: The loss scoreboard in motion
visuals.goal: Show predictions becoming targets and the scalar loss falling.

lessons.objective: By the end you can write a model as nested functions and trace which output depends on which intermediate.

beats.text: One tiny input can pass through several transformations before a prediction appears.
How can we name the route an input takes through a multi-stage model?
Build f(g(x)) from boxes, then change the inner output and watch the outer input change.
Composition means feeding one function's output into the next; order is part of the meaning.
Neural networks are long compositions, so a useful derivative must travel through every stage.
Writing the pipeline explicitly prepares us to measure how changes propagate.

visuals.title: A model as a function pipeline
visuals.goal: Show nested transformations and preserve the order of dependencies.

visuals.title: A model as a function pipeline in motion
visuals.goal: Show nested transformations and preserve the order of dependencies.

lessons.objective: By the end you can interpret a derivative as the local rate of change and read its sign from a curve.

beats.text: At one point a curve can feel flat, steep, uphill, or downhill even when its global shape is complicated.
What number would tell us the immediate effect of nudging the input?
Shrink a secant interval around one point until the line becomes a tangent.
The derivative is the tangent slope: positive means output rises locally, negative means it falls.
Backpropagation will use these local slopes as the small gears that carry sensitivity through a network.
A derivative answers: if this input moves a little right now, how does the output respond?

visuals.title: From secant to tangent
visuals.goal: Make local slope and its sign concrete at a single point.

visuals.title: From secant to tangent in motion
visuals.goal: Make local slope and its sign concrete at a single point.

lessons.objective: By the end you can apply the chain rule to multiply local derivatives through a composition.

beats.text: A change entering a pipeline may be stretched at one gate and shrunk at another.
How can we predict the final change without treating the whole pipeline as a black box?
Track a tiny input change through an inner function and then an outer function.
Each stage contributes a local multiplier, and the total derivative is their product.
The chain rule is the mathematical reason a backward pass can reuse local information.
To find a global sensitivity, multiply the sensitivities encountered along the route.

visuals.title: Sensitivity through chained gates
visuals.goal: Show a perturbation being multiplied by each stage's local derivative.

visuals.title: Sensitivity through chained gates in motion
visuals.goal: Show a perturbation being multiplied by each stage's local derivative.

lessons.objective: By the end you can compute the partial derivative for one coordinate while holding the others fixed.

beats.text: A loss surface has many knobs, and moving two knobs at once hides who caused the change.
How do we isolate one weight's contribution to a multivariable loss?
Freeze every coordinate except one and slice the surface along that direction.
The resulting slope is a partial derivative: one coordinate changes while the rest stay fixed.
Collecting one partial per weight turns a scalar loss surface into a vector of coordinate-wise clues.
Partial derivatives let us ask one precise 'what if this weight moved?' question at a time.

visuals.title: Slicing a loss surface one coordinate at a time
visuals.goal: Show frozen coordinates and the slope measured along one free coordinate.

visuals.title: Slicing a loss surface one coordinate at a time in motion
visuals.goal: Show frozen coordinates and the slope measured along one free coordinate.

lessons.objective: By the end you can assemble partial derivatives into a gradient and explain why its negative points downhill locally.

beats.text: Every coordinate has its own slope, but a model needs one direction for all weights together.
How can several one-coordinate measurements become a single navigation arrow?
Place the partial derivatives into a vector and compare candidate directions on contour lines.
The gradient points toward steepest local increase, so negative gradient points toward steepest local decrease.
Gradient descent uses that arrow as a compass, then tempers it with a learning rate.
The gradient is an uphill compass assembled from partial derivatives; reverse it to descend.

visuals.title: The gradient as an uphill compass
visuals.goal: Connect coordinate slopes to one vector and its reversed downhill direction.

visuals.title: The gradient as an uphill compass in motion
visuals.goal: Connect coordinate slopes to one vector and its reversed downhill direction.

lessons.objective: By the end you can use the gradient descent update and predict how learning rate changes a step.

beats.text: A downhill arrow is useful only when it becomes an actual move through parameter space.
What happens if we subtract the gradient once, twice, or with a much larger multiplier?
Write theta-new equals theta minus learning-rate times gradient and compare step lengths.
Gradient descent recomputes the slope at the new point and repeats; the learning rate scales each move.
Small steps can be slow, while very large steps can overshoot a valley or become unstable.
Direction comes from the negative gradient; distance comes from the learning rate.

visuals.title: Repeated steps down the bowl
visuals.goal: Animate recomputed downhill steps and make learning-rate scaling visible.

visuals.title: Repeated steps down the bowl in motion
visuals.goal: Animate recomputed downhill steps and make learning-rate scaling visible.

visuals.title: Gradient steps down a loss curve
visuals.goal: Vary the learning rate and curvature to see gradient steps converge, overshoot, or diverge.

lessons.objective: By the end you can turn a nested calculation into a computation graph with explicit intermediate dependencies.

beats.text: A long formula hides the small places where values and sensitivities are created.
How could we give every operation a station that remembers what passed through it?
Split a calculation into nodes for inputs, operations, and the final loss, then connect data arrows.
A computation graph records dependencies and creates a route for both forward values and backward sensitivities.
Shared intermediates can fan out, so the graph also tells us where contributions must be combined.
The graph is a navigable map of the calculation, not merely a decorative diagram.

visuals.title: The calculation becomes a graph
visuals.goal: Expose operation nodes, cached intermediates, and dependency arrows.

visuals.title: The calculation becomes a graph in motion
visuals.goal: Expose operation nodes, cached intermediates, and dependency arrows.

lessons.objective: By the end you can trace a forward pass from input through activations to prediction and loss.

beats.text: Training starts with an example moving through the model exactly as it would at inference time.
What values must be known before we can say how wrong the prediction is?
Send an input left to right through each node and leave a checkpoint at every intermediate.
The forward pass computes the prediction and loss while caching values needed by differentiation.
It does not update weights; it creates the evidence that the backward pass will use.
Forward propagation answers what the current weights do on this example.

visuals.title: A signal travels forward
visuals.goal: Show input, activations, prediction, loss, and cached intermediate values in order.

visuals.title: A signal travels forward in motion
visuals.goal: Show input, activations, prediction, loss, and cached intermediate values in order.

lessons.objective: By the end you can explain reverse-mode differentiation as chain-rule sensitivities flowing from loss back to weights.

beats.text: The loss is one scalar, but many upstream operations helped create it.
How can one output error tell every weight how its own nudge would change the loss?
Start with sensitivity one at the loss, then multiply by each local derivative while moving backward.
Reverse mode fans one scalar sensitivity backward and accumulates a gradient for every upstream parameter.
Cached forward values make the local derivatives available without recomputing a separate forward run for every weight.
Backpropagation is the chain rule organized as a reverse walk through the computation graph.

visuals.title: How a network blames its weights
visuals.goal: Show one unit of blame at the loss multiplying through cached local derivatives until every weight has its gradient, then use it for one update.

visuals.title: Blame flows backward
visuals.goal: Make one loss sensitivity fan out into parameter gradients through cached nodes.

visuals.title: Blame flows backward in motion
visuals.goal: Make one loss sensitivity fan out into parameter gradients through cached nodes.

lessons.objective: By the end you can calculate one weight update and explain the role of the learning rate.

beats.text: After the backward pass, every weight has a direction and the optimizer must turn it into a move.
Given a weight, gradient, and learning rate, what should the next weight be?
Substitute values into weight-new equals weight minus learning-rate times gradient and compare rates.
The gradient supplies direction and the learning rate supplies distance; a positive gradient usually lowers loss when subtracted.
Repeat forward pass, backward pass, and update to train across many examples.
Backpropagation finds the local directions; weight updates use those directions to walk the loss landscape.
